--- title: "VAR analysis" subtitle: "Industrial production and University of Michigan consumer sentiment" --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} source("R/setup.R") suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(tseries) # adf.test library(urca) # ur.kpss, ca.jo library(vars) # VARselect, VAR, causality, irf, fevd }) umc_ts <- read_monthly_ts("data/umcsent.csv") fmt_p <- function(p) { if (p < 2.2e-16) return("< 2.2e-16") if (p < 0.001) return(paste("=", format(p, digits = 3, scientific = TRUE))) paste("=", sprintf("%.4f", p)) } # Johansen test statistics next to their critical values johansen_table <- function(jo) { data.frame( Hypothesis = rownames(jo@cval), Statistic = round(jo@teststat, 2), jo@cval, check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL ) } ``` ::: The second series is the University of Michigan Index of Consumer Sentiment (UMCSENT), a monthly survey of how US households see current and future economic conditions. The question is whether consumer sentiment carries information about future industrial production. ## Consumer sentiment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} autoplot(umc_ts) + labs(x = "Year", y = "Index (1966:Q1 = 100)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![University of Michigan consumer sentiment (1966:Q1 = 100)](multivariate_files/figure-html/fig-umcsent-1.png){#fig-umcsent width=768} ::: ::: Unlike industrial production, sentiment has no clear upward trend but large cyclical swings. It falls in the 2001 recession, the 2008–2009 financial crisis and the 2020 pandemic; its lowest value in the sample is 50 (Jun 2022). ## Stationarity of UMCSENT ::: {#tbl-umc-tests .cell tbl-cap='KPSS statistics and ADF p-values, UMCSENT in levels'} ```{.r .cell-code} umc_kpss <- sapply(c(tau = "tau", mu = "mu"), function(type) ur.kpss(umc_ts, type = type)@teststat) adf_lags <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 12, 24) umc_adf <- data.frame( Lag = adf_lags, `ADF p-value` = sapply(adf_lags, function(k) suppressWarnings(adf.test(umc_ts, k = k)$p.value)), check.names = FALSE ) umc_pp <- PP.test(umc_ts) umc_adf ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| Lag| ADF p-value| |---:|-----------:| | 1| 0.0815742| | 2| 0.2458332| | 3| 0.2872010| | 4| 0.3761136| | 5| 0.5352488| | 12| 0.3621571| | 24| 0.3984279|
::: ::: 1. The KPSS statistics (0.3588 with trend and 1.3267 with a constant) are above the 5% critical values (0.146 and 0.463), so stationarity in levels is rejected. 2. All ADF p-values are above 0.05 and the Phillips-Perron test gives p = 0.2266, so the unit root cannot be rejected. All three tests agree: UMCSENT is not stationary in levels. ## Cointegration (Johansen test) Industrial production is not seasonally adjusted, so both the cointegration test and the VAR include **monthly (seasonal) dummy variables** (`season = 12`). Without them, the seasonal pattern ends up in the residuals and distorts the tests. The lag order of the levels VAR used by the Johansen test is chosen with the Akaike information criterion (AIC). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dset <- cbind(ip_ts, umc_ts) colnames(dset) <- c("IPB", "UMCSENT") lag_select <- VARselect(dset, lag.max = 12, type = "const", season = 12) lag_select$selection ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` AIC(n) HQ(n) SC(n) FPE(n) 3 3 1 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} johansen_k <- unname(lag_select$selection["AIC(n)"]) johansen_trace <- ca.jo(dset, type = "trace", ecdet = "const", K = johansen_k, season = 12) johansen_eigen <- ca.jo(dset, type = "eigen", ecdet = "const", K = johansen_k, season = 12) ``` ::: ::: {#tbl-johansen .cell tbl-cap='Johansen test: trace (top) and maximum eigenvalue (bottom)'} ```{.r .cell-code} jo_trace <- johansen_table(johansen_trace) jo_eigen <- johansen_table(johansen_eigen) jo_trace ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Hypothesis | Statistic| 10pct| 5pct| 1pct| |:-------------|---------:|-----:|-----:|-----:| |r <= 1 | | 4.86| 7.52| 9.24| 12.97| |r = 0 | | 16.37| 17.85| 19.96| 24.60|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} jo_eigen ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Hypothesis | Statistic| 10pct| 5pct| 1pct| |:-------------|---------:|-----:|-----:|-----:| |r <= 1 | | 4.86| 7.52| 9.24| 12.97| |r = 0 | | 11.51| 13.75| 15.67| 20.20|
::: ::: With K = 3 lags, for r = 0 both the trace statistic (16.37) and the maximum eigenvalue statistic (11.51) are below their 5% critical values (19.96 and 15.67). The null hypothesis r = 0 cannot be rejected: there is no cointegrating relationship, so no stable long-run link between industrial production and consumer sentiment. A VECM is therefore not estimated; instead, a VAR is fitted to the first differences of both series to make them stationary. ## First differences ::: {#tbl-diff-tests .cell tbl-cap='ADF and Phillips-Perron p-values for the differenced series'} ```{.r .cell-code} dset_diff <- data.frame( IPB_d = diff(as.numeric(ip_ts)), UMCSENT_d = diff(as.numeric(umc_ts)) ) diff_tests <- data.frame( Series = names(dset_diff), `ADF p-value` = sapply(dset_diff, function(x) suppressWarnings(adf.test(x)$p.value)), `PP p-value` = sapply(dset_diff, function(x) PP.test(x)$p.value), check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL ) diff_tests ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Series | ADF p-value| PP p-value| |:---------|-----------:|----------:| |IPB_d | 0.01| 0.01| |UMCSENT_d | 0.01| 0.01|
::: ::: For both differenced series the ADF and Phillips-Perron p-values are 0.01 (below 0.05), so the unit root is rejected: both series are stationary after differencing and can be used in the VAR. ## VAR lag selection and estimation The VAR is estimated on the first differences with a constant and monthly dummies. The lag order should leave residuals free of autocorrelation; otherwise the Granger tests and the impulse response bands are not reliable. The table below shows the Portmanteau test for every lag order from 1 to 12. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} var_lag <- VARselect(dset_diff, lag.max = 12, type = "const", season = 12) var_lag$selection ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` AIC(n) HQ(n) SC(n) FPE(n) 12 2 2 12 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-var-lags .cell tbl-cap='Portmanteau test (20 lags) on the VAR residuals, by lag order'} ```{.r .cell-code} lag_check <- data.frame( `Lag order` = 1:12, `Portmanteau p-value` = sapply(1:12, function(p) { v <- VAR(dset_diff, p = p, type = "const", season = 12) serial.test(v, lags.pt = 20, type = "PT.asymptotic")$serial$p.value }), check.names = FALSE ) lag_check[["Portmanteau p-value"]] <- round(lag_check[["Portmanteau p-value"]], 4) lag_check ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| Lag order| Portmanteau p-value| |---------:|-------------------:| | 1| 0.0000| | 2| 0.0013| | 3| 0.0086| | 4| 0.0094| | 5| 0.0318| | 6| 0.0471| | 7| 0.0439| | 8| 0.0316| | 9| 0.0177| | 10| 0.0344| | 11| 0.0249| | 12| 0.4359|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} var_p <- unname(var_lag$selection["AIC(n)"]) var_model <- VAR(dset_diff, p = var_p, type = "const", season = 12) ``` ::: The Schwarz and Hannan-Quinn criteria choose 2 lags, but with fewer than 12 lags the residuals remain autocorrelated at the 5% level. The AIC choice, p = 12, removes the autocorrelation and is used below. Twelve lags of monthly data cover one full year, which is plausible for a non-seasonally adjusted series. ::: {#tbl-var-ipb .cell tbl-cap='Equation for the change in industrial production (IPB_d): lags of UMCSENT_d'} ```{.r .cell-code} var_summary <- summary(var_model) ipb_eq <- var_summary$varresult$IPB_d$coefficients umc_eq <- var_summary$varresult$UMCSENT_d$coefficients as.data.frame(round(ipb_eq[grep("^UMCSENT_d", rownames(ipb_eq)), ], 4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| | Estimate| Std. Error| t value| Pr(>|t|)| |:-------------|--------:|----------:|-------:|------------------:| |UMCSENT_d.l1 | 0.0555| 0.0138| 4.0216| 0.0001| |UMCSENT_d.l2 | -0.0182| 0.0141| -1.2884| 0.1984| |UMCSENT_d.l3 | 0.0175| 0.0145| 1.2123| 0.2262| |UMCSENT_d.l4 | 0.0044| 0.0144| 0.3049| 0.7606| |UMCSENT_d.l5 | 0.0074| 0.0144| 0.5132| 0.6081| |UMCSENT_d.l6 | 0.0084| 0.0143| 0.5835| 0.5599| |UMCSENT_d.l7 | 0.0168| 0.0143| 1.1763| 0.2402| |UMCSENT_d.l8 | 0.0147| 0.0142| 1.0375| 0.3002| |UMCSENT_d.l9 | 0.0043| 0.0141| 0.3050| 0.7605| |UMCSENT_d.l10 | 0.0388| 0.0141| 2.7565| 0.0061| |UMCSENT_d.l11 | -0.0088| 0.0140| -0.6299| 0.5291| |UMCSENT_d.l12 | 0.0133| 0.0140| 0.9493| 0.3431|
::: ::: ::: {#tbl-var-umc .cell tbl-cap='Equation for the change in consumer sentiment (UMCSENT_d): lags of IPB_d'} ```{.r .cell-code} umc_on_ipb <- umc_eq[grep("^IPB_d", rownames(umc_eq)), ] n_sig_ipb_lags <- sum(umc_on_ipb[, "Pr(>|t|)"] < 0.05) as.data.frame(round(umc_on_ipb, 4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| | Estimate| Std. Error| t value| Pr(>|t|)| |:---------|--------:|----------:|-------:|------------------:| |IPB_d.l1 | 0.2776| 0.1881| 1.4755| 0.1409| |IPB_d.l2 | 0.0706| 0.1896| 0.3723| 0.7099| |IPB_d.l3 | 0.1825| 0.1907| 0.9569| 0.3392| |IPB_d.l4 | -0.1169| 0.1913| -0.6108| 0.5417| |IPB_d.l5 | 0.1638| 0.1904| 0.8601| 0.3903| |IPB_d.l6 | -0.0806| 0.1903| -0.4236| 0.6721| |IPB_d.l7 | 0.0377| 0.1900| 0.1985| 0.8427| |IPB_d.l8 | -0.2658| 0.1899| -1.3995| 0.1625| |IPB_d.l9 | 0.1141| 0.1907| 0.5984| 0.5499| |IPB_d.l10 | 0.0146| 0.1906| 0.0766| 0.9390| |IPB_d.l11 | -0.0982| 0.1879| -0.5227| 0.6015| |IPB_d.l12 | -0.4202| 0.1839| -2.2857| 0.0228|
::: ::: 1. In the industrial production equation, sentiment one month earlier (`UMCSENT_d.l1`) has a positive coefficient (0.055) that is highly significant (p = 6.99e-05): an improvement in consumer confidence is followed by higher industrial production the next month. 2. In the sentiment equation, only 1 of the 12 lags of industrial production is significant at 5%, about what chance alone would produce. ## VAR diagnostics ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} var_serial <- serial.test(var_model, lags.pt = 20, type = "PT.asymptotic") var_arch <- vars::arch.test(var_model, lags.multi = 12, multivariate.only = TRUE) var_norm <- normality.test(var_model, multivariate.only = TRUE) diag_p <- c( var_serial$serial$p.value, var_arch$arch.mul$p.value, var_norm$jb.mul$JB$p.value ) data.frame( Test = c("Portmanteau (autocorrelation, 20 lags)", "Multivariate ARCH (12 lags)", "Jarque-Bera (normality)"), `p-value` = sub("^= ", "", sapply(diag_p, fmt_p)), check.names = FALSE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Test |p-value | |:--------------------------------------|:---------| |Portmanteau (autocorrelation, 20 lags) |0.4359 | |Multivariate ARCH (12 lags) |8.14e-08 | |Jarque-Bera (normality) |< 2.2e-16 |
::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} stability_model <- stability(var_model, type = "OLS-CUSUM") plot(stability_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![OLS-CUSUM stability test for each VAR equation](multivariate_files/figure-html/fig-cusum-1.png){#fig-cusum width=768} ::: ::: 1. **Autocorrelation:** the Portmanteau test gives p = 0.4359, so the residuals show no remaining autocorrelation. 2. **ARCH effects and non-normality:** both tests give p < 0.05. The residual variance changes over time and the distribution has heavy tails, reflecting the 2008–2009 and 2020 shocks. The coefficient estimates remain consistent, but standard errors and p-values rely on large-sample approximations and should be read with some caution. 3. **Stability:** in the OLS-CUSUM plot, the empirical fluctuation process stays within the critical bands for both equations, so there is no evidence of a structural break in the parameters. This is a separate property: it does not compensate for the ARCH effects above. ## Granger causality ::: {#tbl-granger .cell tbl-cap='Granger causality tests (F-tests on all lags of the causing variable)'} ```{.r .cell-code} granger_ipb <- causality(var_model, cause = "IPB_d") granger_umc <- causality(var_model, cause = "UMCSENT_d") data.frame( Direction = c("IPB_d -> UMCSENT_d", "UMCSENT_d -> IPB_d"), `F statistic` = round(c(granger_ipb$Granger$statistic, granger_umc$Granger$statistic), 4), `p-value` = round(c(granger_ipb$Granger$p.value, granger_umc$Granger$p.value), 4), check.names = FALSE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Direction | F statistic| p-value| |:------------------|-----------:|-------:| |IPB_d -> UMCSENT_d | 1.0258| 0.4227| |UMCSENT_d -> IPB_d | 2.5253| 0.0029|
::: ::: 1. IPB_d → UMCSENT_d: p = 0.4227 (> 0.05); changes in industrial production do not help predict consumer sentiment. 2. UMCSENT_d → IPB_d: the joint p-value for the 12 lags is 0.0029 (< 0.05), so the null hypothesis of no Granger causality is rejected: past changes in consumer sentiment help predict changes in industrial production. The relationship is one-directional: sentiment helps to predict industrial production, but not the other way round. Granger causality is about predictive content, not about economic causation. ::: {.callout-note} In an earlier version of this analysis, the VAR had 4 lags and no seasonal dummies; its residuals were autocorrelated and the Granger test for UMCSENT_d → IPB_d was not significant (p = 0.18). Accounting for seasonality and choosing the lag order so that the residuals are clean changes this result. ::: ## Impulse response functions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(123) # bootstrap confidence bands irf_umc_to_ipb <- irf( var_model, impulse = "UMCSENT_d", response = "IPB_d", n.ahead = 20, boot = TRUE, ci = 0.90 ) plot(irf_umc_to_ipb, main = "Shock to UMCSENT_d, response of IPB_d") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Response of IPB_d to a shock in UMCSENT_d (90% bootstrap bands)](multivariate_files/figure-html/fig-irf-umc-1.png){#fig-irf-umc width=768} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} irf_ipb_to_umc <- irf( var_model, impulse = "IPB_d", response = "UMCSENT_d", n.ahead = 20, boot = TRUE, ci = 0.90 ) plot(irf_ipb_to_umc, main = "Shock to IPB_d, response of UMCSENT_d") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Response of UMCSENT_d to a shock in IPB_d (90% bootstrap bands)](multivariate_files/figure-html/fig-irf-ipb-1.png){#fig-irf-ipb width=768} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Horizons (months after the shock) at which the 90% band excludes zero significant_horizons <- function(x, impulse) { which(x$Lower[[impulse]][, 1] > 0 | x$Upper[[impulse]][, 1] < 0) - 1 } and_list <- function(x) { if (length(x) == 0) return("at no horizon") if (length(x) == 1) return(as.character(x)) paste(paste(head(x, -1), collapse = ", "), "and", tail(x, 1)) } sig_umc_to_ipb <- significant_horizons(irf_umc_to_ipb, "UMCSENT_d") sig_ipb_to_umc <- significant_horizons(irf_ipb_to_umc, "IPB_d") ``` ::: 1. A positive shock to consumer sentiment raises industrial production one month later (response of 0.22 index points, with the bootstrap band entirely above zero). Over the 20 months shown, the band excludes zero only 1 and 10 months after the shock, so the effect is concentrated in the first month and is short-lived. 2. For a shock to industrial production, the band excludes zero only 12 months after the shock: production shocks have essentially no effect on consumer confidence. With 90% bands, about 2 of 20 horizons are expected to exclude zero by chance alone, so isolated significant points far from the shock should not be over-interpreted. ### Robustness: variable ordering and cumulative effect The impulse responses above are *orthogonalised* with a Cholesky decomposition, which requires an ordering of the variables. With industrial production first, a sentiment shock cannot move production in the same month by construction. Below, the VAR is re-estimated with sentiment first, and the **cumulative** responses are computed: since the VAR is in first differences, the cumulative response of `IPB_d` is the effect on the *level* of the index. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} var_model_rev <- VAR(dset_diff[, c("UMCSENT_d", "IPB_d")], p = var_p, type = "const", season = 12) set.seed(123) irf_rev <- irf(var_model_rev, impulse = "UMCSENT_d", response = "IPB_d", n.ahead = 12, boot = TRUE, ci = 0.90) cumulative_irf <- function(model) { set.seed(123) irf(model, impulse = "UMCSENT_d", response = "IPB_d", n.ahead = 12, boot = TRUE, ci = 0.90, cumulative = TRUE) } cum_base <- cumulative_irf(var_model) cum_rev <- cumulative_irf(var_model_rev) # Size of a one-standard-deviation orthogonal sentiment shock, in index points shock_size <- function(model, var) { chol_factor <- t(chol(summary(model)$covres)) chol_factor[var, var] } resid_corr <- summary(var_model)$corres["IPB_d", "UMCSENT_d"] ``` ::: ::: {#tbl-irf-robustness .cell tbl-cap='Response of industrial production to a sentiment shock under both orderings (90% bootstrap bands)'} ```{.r .cell-code} irf_row <- function(x, step, label, ordering) { data.frame( Ordering = ordering, Measure = label, Response = round(x$irf$UMCSENT_d[step + 1, 1], 3), `Lower 90%` = round(x$Lower$UMCSENT_d[step + 1, 1], 3), `Upper 90%` = round(x$Upper$UMCSENT_d[step + 1, 1], 3), check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL ) } rbind( irf_row(irf_umc_to_ipb, 0, "Same month", "Production first"), irf_row(irf_umc_to_ipb, 1, "After 1 month", "Production first"), irf_row(cum_base, 12, "Cumulative, 12 months", "Production first"), irf_row(irf_rev, 0, "Same month", "Sentiment first"), irf_row(irf_rev, 1, "After 1 month", "Sentiment first"), irf_row(cum_rev, 12, "Cumulative, 12 months", "Sentiment first") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Ordering |Measure | Response| Lower 90%| Upper 90%| |:----------------|:---------------------|--------:|---------:|---------:| |Production first |Same month | 0.000| 0.000| 0.000| |Production first |After 1 month | 0.223| 0.138| 0.305| |Production first |Cumulative, 12 months | 0.388| 0.104| 0.674| |Sentiment first |Same month | 0.097| -0.066| 0.361| |Sentiment first |After 1 month | 0.237| 0.152| 0.341| |Sentiment first |Cumulative, 12 months | 0.502| 0.166| 0.869|
::: ::: 1. The residuals of the two equations are only weakly correlated (correlation 0.09), so the ordering matters little. With sentiment first, the same-month response is 0.1 and its band includes zero; the response after one month (0.24) remains significant. 2. A one-standard-deviation sentiment shock (about 4 index points of sentiment) raises the **level** of industrial production by 0.39 index points after 12 months (90% band 0.1 to 0.67), or 0.5 with sentiment ordered first. The effect is statistically significant but economically small: the index is around 100, so this is roughly half a percent. This supports the view of sentiment indicators as leading indicators of real industrial activity. ## Forecast error variance decomposition ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fevd_result <- fevd(var_model, n.ahead = 10) plot(fevd_result) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Forecast error variance decomposition (10 months)](multivariate_files/figure-html/fig-fevd-1.png){#fig-fevd width=768} ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-fevd .cell tbl-cap='Share of forecast error variance at a 10-month horizon'} ```{.r .cell-code} fevd_10 <- rbind( IPB_d = fevd_result$IPB_d[10, ], UMCSENT_d = fevd_result$UMCSENT_d[10, ] ) as.data.frame(round(100 * fevd_10, 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| | IPB_d| UMCSENT_d| |:---------|-----:|---------:| |IPB_d | 95.20| 4.80| |UMCSENT_d | 1.94| 98.06|
::: ::: 1. In the first month, almost 100% of the variance of each variable is explained by its own shocks. 2. At a 10-month horizon, changes in consumer sentiment explain about 4.8% of the forecast error variance of industrial production. 3. In the other direction, industrial production explains only 1.94% of the variance of consumer sentiment. The decomposition supports a one-sided relationship: sentiment explains a modest share of the forecast uncertainty of industrial production, while the reverse share is negligible. ## VAR forecast ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} var_forecast <- predict(var_model, n.ahead = 24, ci = 0.90) fc_ipb_diff <- var_forecast$fcst$IPB_d[, "fcst"] # Rebuild index levels by adding the forecast changes to the last observed value last_ipb <- tail(as.numeric(ip_ts), 1) fc_ipb_level <- cumsum(c(last_ipb, fc_ipb_diff))[-1] history_time <- as.numeric(time(ip_ts)) last_time_point <- tail(history_time, 1) forecast_time <- seq(last_time_point + 1 / 12, by = 1 / 12, length.out = length(fc_ipb_level)) df_ipb <- data.frame( time = c(history_time, forecast_time), value = c(as.numeric(ip_ts), fc_ipb_level) ) ggplot(df_ipb, aes(x = time, y = value)) + geom_line() + geom_vline(xintercept = last_time_point, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") + labs(x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![VAR forecast of industrial production, 24 months ahead (dashed line = end of data)](multivariate_files/figure-html/fig-var-forecast-1.png){#fig-var-forecast width=768} ::: ::: 1. `predict()` forecasts the next 24 months with a 90% interval. 2. Because the VAR is estimated on differences, the forecasts are monthly changes. 3. They are converted back to index levels with `cumsum()`, adding the forecast changes to the last observed value (99.33). 4. To the right of the dashed red line, the forecast reproduces the seasonal pattern through the monthly dummies. On average it stays around 101.6 index points over the 24 months and ends at 100.68, close to the recent level of the series.
